ap-econ-micro/index.content:
AP Microeconomics
High-difficulty concepts and logic-heavy modules. Optimized for quick reference before exams.

I. Basic Concepts

Economics: The study of how societies allocate scarce resources to produce and distribute goods.
Macroeconomics: Overall economic performance — inflation, GDP, unemployment.
Microeconomics: Behavior of individual entities — firms and households.
Positive Economics: Describes facts. “What is.”
Normative Economics: Involves value judgments. “What ought to be.”

Scarcity & Opportunity Cost

Scarcity: Limited resources (Land, Labor, Capital, Entrepreneurship) cannot meet unlimited wants.
Opportunity Cost: The value of the next best alternative foregone.


II. Economic Systems & Models
The Three Fundamental Questions

What to produce?
How to produce?
For whom to produce?

Circular Flow Model

Product Market: Households are buyers; Firms are sellers.
Factor Market: Firms are buyers; Households are sellers.



III. Utility & Elasticity
Utility Maximizing Rule
A rational consumer allocates income so the last dollar spent on each good yields equal Marginal Utility:
\frac{MU_x}{P_x} = \frac{MU_y}{P_y}
Elasticity Formulas






























TypeFormulaKey LogicPED%ΔQd / %ΔP> 1 Elastic · = 1 Unit Elastic (TR is max)PES%ΔQs / %ΔPSeller responsiveness to price changesYED%ΔQd / %ΔIncome> 0 Normal Good · < 0 Inferior GoodXED%ΔQdA / %ΔPb> 0 Substitutes · < 0 Complements

IV. Product Market Efficiency
Productive Efficiency
“How to produce.” Production occurs at the lowest possible cost.
P = \min ATC
At this point resources are used with zero waste. In the long run, perfectly competitive firms are forced here.

Allocative Efficiency
“What to produce.” Resources yield the mix of goods most wanted by society.
P = MC

Price (P) represents Marginal Benefit — the value society places on the last unit.
Marginal Cost (MC) represents Opportunity Cost — the value of alternatives sacrificed.





















ConditionMeaningImplicationP > MCUnder-allocationMB > MC; increase output (common in monopoly)P < MCOver-allocationMB < MC; reduce output


V. Market Structures
Natural Monopoly
Continuous economies of scale — ATC is a downward slope.
ATC = \frac{TFC}{Q} + AVC

























RegulationRuleResultUnregulatedMR = MCProfit max; highest price; large DWLFair ReturnP = ATCNormal profit (break-even)Socially OptimalP = MCAllocative efficiency; firm runs at a loss

Monopolistic Competition

Short Run: Behaves like a monopoly — profit or loss.
Long Run: Entry/exit shifts demand until P = ATC (tangent point).
Inefficiency: Always has excess capacity (not at min ATC) and P > MC.



VI. Factor Market
Hiring Rule
A firm hires until:
MRP = MFC

MRP (Marginal Revenue Product): MP \times P — the benefit of one more unit of labor.
MFC (Marginal Factor Cost): \Delta TC / \Delta L — the cost of one more unit of labor.

Monopsony
Single buyer of labor. MFC > Supply (Wage) because hiring one more worker raises the wage for all workers.
Decision: Find Q where MRP = MFC, then trace down to the supply curve for the wage.

Least-Cost Combination
\frac{MP_L}{P_L} = \frac{MP_K}{P_K}

VII. Market Failures & Externalities

mkt-inbound/index.title: Inbound Marketing
mkt-inbound/index.content:
Inbound Marketing
A systemic framework for growth — from buyer psychology to martech infrastructure.

I. Buyer Personas: Motivations Over Demographics
A buyer persona is a model of an ideal customer built on Buying Insights, not just demographic data.

Buying Insights as the Core: Personas are built on priority initiatives, success factors, and perceived barriers — the why behind a decision.
The Hero’s Journey: Marketing acts as a guide for a prospect on a quest to solve specific challenges.
Strategic Exclusion: Negative Personas filter out low-fit leads, concentrating resources on high-value segments.
Journey Alignment: Content must match the buyer’s cognitive state — from awareness of a symptom → evaluation of solution categories → vendor selection.


II. Behavioral Analysis: Signal Detection & Segmentation
Behavioral marketing treats user actions as data points for intent and timing.

Interaction Tracking: High-intent signals include CTA engagement, time on technical pages, and visit frequency.
Intent Thresholds: Quantitative triggers for personalized follow-up (e.g., three visits to a landing page without converting).





















Segmentation TypeSourceExampleImplicit (Correlation)Inferred from behaviorIdentifying a “dog owner” from browsing patternsExplicit (Causation)Provided directly by the userForm submissions, account creation

III. Attribution & Testing
Marketing as iterative science — every outcome backed by a statistical model.
Attribution Models

























ModelLogicBest ForFirst Touch100% credit to first contactDemand generation analysisTime DecayMore credit as events approach conversionShort sales cycle analysisFull-PathCredits first touch, lead creation, and final dealHolistic revenue funnel view
The Bullets vs. Cannonballs Methodology

Bullets: Low-risk A/B tests to validate a single hypothesis.
Cannonballs: High-resource investments made only after a bullet provides evidence of success.

Statistical Significance

Variable Isolation: Test one independent variable at a time.
Confidence Threshold: Results held to 95% confidence to rule out random variance.


IV. Martech & Automation Infrastructure
Growth at scale requires a centralized stack for data integrity.

CRM as Data Hub: Single source of truth — all teams share the same context on a buyer’s state.
Automation as Force Multiplier: Beyond email sequences, automation should trigger internal record updates and sales alerts based on behavioral intent thresholds.



Ready for the exam? → Mastery Challenge

mkt-inbound/mastery-challenge.title: Mastery Challenge
mkt-inbound/mastery-challenge.content:
Inbound Marketing — Mastery Challenge
15 logic-based questions. If you can answer these comfortably and with understanding of the underlying reasoning, you are well-prepared for the HubSpot Inbound Marketing Certification.

I. Methodology & Infrastructure


The Magnetism Shift — Inbound marketing attracts customers through tailored experiences rather than interruption. How does this customer-centric mindset fundamentally change how you approach a prospect compared to traditional outbound methods?


The Digital Nervous System — A CRM is the heart of a marketing stack. Why is it impossible to scale an inbound strategy effectively without a centralized system of record?



II. Personas


Beyond Demographics — Meaningful buyer personas are built on “buying insights,” not demographics. Why is understanding the why behind a purchase more critical for content creation than knowing a user’s age or location?


The Power of “No” — Creating “negative personas” is a key part of research. How does identifying who you don’t want to attract help optimize marketing ROI?


Humanizing Data — HubSpot suggests curating a story to humanize your persona. How does turning a trait list into a narrative change how your entire team interacts with potential leads?



III. The Buyer’s Journey


Cognitive Alignment — Content must map to Awareness, Consideration, and Decision stages. How would your strategy differ when a buyer is defining their problem versus evaluating specific solutions?


The Frictionless Action — Every piece of content needs a Call to Action. What questions should you ask to ensure your content actually prompts action rather than passive consumption?



IV. Distribution & Validation


Channel Synergy — Inbound balances owned, earned, and paid channels. In what scenario would you prioritize an earned channel over a paid one to build long-term trust?


Scientific Rigor — Why is relying on a raw conversion increase dangerous if results aren’t statistically significant?



V. Behavioral Intelligence


Decoding Intent — Implicit segmentation tracks what users do; explicit tracks what they tell you. Which type provides a more honest signal of immediate intent, and why?


The Multichannel Approach — How do you maintain a consistent message when a user interacts with your brand across three different platforms?



VI. Attribution & Experiments


The Credit Problem — How does the “Time Decay” model specifically credit touchpoints as a buyer gets closer to conversion?


Predictive Strategy — Attribution isn’t just about reporting the past. How can understanding attribution data inform future budget allocation decisions?



VII. Automation & Scale


The Hygiene Prerequisite — How does poor data quality directly sabotage an automated email nurturing sequence?


The Human-Machine Balance — How can a poorly timed automated cadence negatively impact the customer experience even when the content itself is valuable?

yale-psyc-110/index.title: Yale PSYC 110
yale-psyc-110/index.content:
PSYC 110 — Introduction to Psychology
Textbook: Peter Gray’s Psychology, 5th ed. · Short Readings: The Norton Reader, ed. Gary Marcus

Lecture 0 | Introduction
Two competing frameworks for understanding the mind:

















FrameworkViewIntuitive Psychology (Dualism)Mind (soul) and body (physical matter) are distinct entities.Scientific Psychology (Materialism)All mental events are products of neuronal activity.

Lecture 1 | Foundations: The Neuron & Brain
The Neuron

You’re nothing but a pack of neurons. — Lewis Carroll’s Alice


All-or-None Law: A neuron either fires a full electrical impulse or not at all — analogous to binary code.
Neurotransmitters: Chemical messengers released into the synapse to communicate between cells.

Brain Structure

















RegionFunctionSubcortical StructuresBasic instincts and drivesCerebral CortexReasoning, language, perception

Hemispheric Specialization: Left brain → logic and language; right brain → spatial and holistic perception.
Split-Brain: When the corpus callosum is severed, visual fields and movements lose coordination between hemispheres.


Lecture 3 | Foundations: Freud
The Structure of Mind
Freud saw personality as a constant conflict between three forces, all driven by unconscious motivation:





























StructureNicknamePrincipleRoleIdThe ChildPleasure PrincipleSeeks immediate gratification (hunger, sex, aggression)SuperegoThe JudgeMoral PrincipleInternal compass learned from parents and societyEgoThe MediatorReality PrincipleSatisfies the Id in ways acceptable to the Superego
Psychosexual Stages of Development
Freud argued personality is shaped by how libidinal energy is handled in childhood:

Oral — Focus on the mouth (sucking, eating).
Anal — Focus on control and cleanliness (toilet training).
Phallic — Focus on sexual identity; Oedipus complex. (Penis envy occurs here in Freud’s theory.)
Latency — Sexual drives are repressed; a quiet developmental period.
Genital — Mature adult sexuality (puberty onward).

Defense Mechanisms
The Ego uses these strategies to reduce anxiety from the Id–Superego conflict:






























MechanismDefinitionExampleDisplacementRedirecting impulses to a safer targetAngry at your father; kick the dog insteadProjectionAttributing your own thoughts to othersA man with sexual urges accuses others of thinking about sexRationalizationConstructing logical excuses for bad behavior”I hit the child for their own good”RegressionReverting to childish behavior under stressAn adult throwing a tantrum
Scientific Criticism

Sexism: Concepts like penis envy are widely regarded as culturally biased.
Unfalsifiability: Freudian theories cannot be empirically tested or disproven — disqualifying them as scientific by modern standards.
The Legacy: Despite these flaws, Freud correctly emphasized that the unconscious mind and early childhood experiences have profound influence on adult behavior.


Lecture 4 | Foundations: Skinner & Behaviorism
More on the Unconscious (Freud cont.)
Most mental activity is unconscious. This has evolutionary roots — humans are wired to:

Deceive others to appear more favorable.
Detect when others are deceiving them.
Believe their own best lies (children who “truly believe” in their sadness give more authentic performances).

Behaviorism
Key figures: John B. Watson · B. F. Skinner
Core propositions:

All behavior is derived from learning — no innate nature.
Only observable behavior matters; internal mental states are not studied.
Humans and animals are fundamentally the same in learning mechanisms.

Learning Mechanisms


Habituation — Learning to ignore irrelevant or repeated stimuli.


Classical Conditioning (Ivan Pavlov) — neutral stimulus + unconditioned stimulus → conditioned response

Extinction: Response fades when the conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented without the unconditioned stimulus.
Spontaneous Recovery: Extinguished response reappears after a rest period.
Generalization: Response transfers to stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus.



Operant Conditioning (Skinner) — Consequences shape future behavior.

Reward → behavior increases.
Punishment → behavior decreases.


























TypeDefinitionExamplePositive ReinforcementAdd a rewardGive a treat for sittingNegative ReinforcementRemove something aversiveTurn off alarm when you wake upPunishmentAdd something aversiveFine for speeding

Note: Negative Reinforcement ≠ Punishment. Negative reinforcement increases behavior by removing something unpleasant.


Shaping: Reinforcing successive approximations toward a target behavior.
Partial Reinforcement: Intermittent schedules produce more resistant behavior than continuous reinforcement.



Criticisms of Behaviorism
Behaviorism is considered too extreme — it ignores cognition, emotion, and biological predispositions entirely. ↩ Back to core propositions
